questions.q: A strategy wins {w}% of trades. Wins average {a}R and losses average 1R. What's its expectancy per trade, in R? (Minus sign if negative.)
A strategy that wins 90% of its trades must be profitable.
questions.why: If the 10% of losses are huge (say 20R each), it loses money overall. Expectancy needs win rate and the size of wins and losses.

questions.q: A strategy's expectancy is {e}R per trade before costs. Spreads and fees cost {c}R per trade. What's the expectancy after costs?
questions.why: Costs come straight off: {e}R − {c}R = {answer}R. A small edge can disappear entirely.

questions.q: A strategy wins 40% of the time. Over 100 trades, how likely is at least one run of 6 losses in a row?
questions.why: With a 60% chance of losing each trade, long losing runs are normal. Plan your risk for them.

questions.q: Which is a warning sign that a backtested strategy is overfitted?
options: It does brilliantly with a 17-day average but terribly with 16 or 18
It uses simple rules with a clear reason
It was tested on hundreds of trades across rising and falling markets
It performs similarly on data it wasn't designed on
questions.why: Results that collapse when a setting is nudged suggest the rules fit past noise, not a real pattern.

questions.q: Put the steps of honest testing in order.
items: Write exact rules before looking at results
Backtest on one period, taking every signal and including costs
Run the final rules once on data you held back
questions.why: Rules first, then in-sample testing, then out-of-sample, then real time.

questions.q: Match each testing mistake to its description.
pairs: Tuning rules until they fit past noise
Testing only on companies that still exist
Using information you couldn't have had at the time
Showing only the period where it worked
questions.why: Each one makes a backtest look better than reality.

questions.q: Which of these is a testable strategy rule?
options: Buy at the close when price closes above its 20-day high and above the 50-day moving average
Buy when I have a good feeling
Buy shares that are popular this week
questions.why: It's exact enough that anyone following it would take the same trades, so it can be tested.

questions.q: Ten winning trades in a backtest is strong proof of an edge.
questions.why: Ten trades can easily come from luck. You need dozens to hundreds, across different conditions.

questions.q: Explain what overfitting is and why an overfitted strategy fails on new data.

ideas.label: Tweaking rules or settings until they fit past data perfectly
It captures past noise or luck rather than a real pattern, so it doesn't repeat

questions.model: Overfitting is tweaking rules and settings until they fit past data perfectly. The rules end up describing that data's random noise and luck rather than a real, repeatable pattern, so on new data the noise is different and the strategy fails.
questions.why: Fitting noise looks like skill until the noise changes.

tests.answer: It's tweaking the settings until they fit the past perfectly, so it captures random noise that won't repeat on new data.
Tweaking the settings until the backtest looks perfect.
When a trader eats too much.

questions.q: Explain why you shouldn't abandon a well-tested strategy after six losses in a row.

ideas.label: Long losing runs are normal and expected, even with a positive expectancy
Judge it over many trades; with small risk per trade the run is survivable

questions.model: With a 40% win rate, six losses in a row is very likely somewhere in 100 trades, so it's normal, not a sign the strategy is broken. It should be judged on expectancy over many trades, and with 1% risk per trade the run only costs about 6% of the account.
questions.why: Streaks are part of the maths, not proof of failure.

tests.answer: Losing streaks are normal even with positive expectancy, so judge it over many trades and keep risk at 1%.
Because the next trade must win.
